title: Flowers and their insect visitors become mutually adapted

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Flowers and their insect visitors become mutually adapted

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: A flower and a bee can slowly become modified and adapted to each other, at the same time or one after the other, by the continued preservation of individuals with mutually favourable slight differences in structure.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Thus I can understand how a flower and a bee might slowly become, either simultaneously or one after the other, modified and adapted in the most perfect manner to each other, by the continued preservation of individuals presenting mutual and slightly favourable deviations of structure.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter IV, “Natural Selection”; section “Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes”. Scope: flowering plants and their insect pollinators

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch04-09: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.61

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Mutual adaptation has measurable component predictions and substantial public interaction data. Existing data are strongest for selected networks and often cannot distinguish coevolution from one-sided adaptation.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Map floral and pollinator structural traits, interaction effectiveness and phylogenies, then test reciprocal trait matching and correlated evolutionary change. Reciprocal fitness benefits and repeated correlated shifts support mutual adaptation; matching explained solely by shared environment or one-sided adaptation weakens it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Trait matching can result from ecological filtering rather than coevolution.

Interaction databases rarely include reciprocal fitness effects or fine structural measurements.

fields.value:

discriminating power: 0.55

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Trait matching and correlated phylogenetic change are standard tests, and interaction networks plus floral traits make a partial version feasible. Coverage is a subset of flowering plants and their insects, concentrated where networks have been assembled. Matching alone does not show that both parties were modified, or whether the changes were simultaneous, so the analysis discriminates mutual adaptation only modestly from one-sided filtering.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Match floral measurements to the morphology of recorded insect visitors and test whether changes on the two phylogenies are correlated. Trait matching beyond a null of random visits would support mutual modification; matching explained entirely by pollinators filtering flowers that already fit would refute reciprocal adaptation. Simultaneous versus sequential change is a further, weaker contrast using relative timing on time-calibrated trees.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
One-sided adaptation and ecological filtering produce trait matching without reciprocal change.

Network coverage is strong for a few floras and poor for most insect-plant pairs.

Visitor morphology and corolla measurements are only partly in the same databases as interactions.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

discriminating power: 0.54
data adequacy: 0.44
analysis feasibility: 0.58
data existence: 0.66
